items.title: @rohanpaul_ai：New HuggingFace paper argues that increasing agent autonomy can gradually make human oversight ineffective by causing ap
items.abstract_or_text: New HuggingFace paper argues that increasing agent autonomy can gradually make human oversight ineffective by causing approval fatigue, overreliance, loss of situational awareness, and skill degradation. As agents do more, users are pushed into approval mode: skimming plans, granting permissions, and reconstructing what happened across steps. Over time, automation bias, approval fatigue, weaker situational awareness, and skill atrophy can make those approvals less reliable. Worse, weak approvals can become training or evaluation signals, rewarding systems for being easy to approve rather than easy to scrutinize. Their answer is cognitive scaffolding at 2 levels: developers add strategic friction, better approval design, behavioral monitoring, and checks that force attention at consequential moments. – arxiv. org/abs/2608.23642 Title: "AI Agents Push Humans Out of the Loop"

items.title: @aimalysheva：meet @mostik_ai! what happens when you put 12 PhDs in one room for four months? first place on the ARC-AGI leaderboard,
items.abstract_or_text: meet @mostik_ai! what happens when you put 12 PhDs in one room for four months? first place on the ARC-AGI leaderboard, which I can't say much about while the competition is still running. and this, which I can. everyone's arguing about whether open models will catch up to frontier models. we think it's the wrong question. here's the one we pose: why does a frontier model have to generate your answer at all, when the only thing you need from it is the reasoning? we do this by enabling models to communicate in latent space. through our protocol, hidden states pass straight from a frontier model into a small one running on your infrastructure -- no text between them, and neither model is fine-tuned. two models from different families, sharing reasoning, both left untouched. how do we know it works? we tested it on a setup where a 753B model reads the problem, and a 4B edge-class model writes the answer. with this approach, we get results 80% as accurate as the frontier model, but at 20x faster performance. we're committed to preventing frontier model lock-in and are already partnering with inference providers to accelerate open-weight adoption. we've done this between 15 of us, in four months, 12 PhDs and a Fields medalist, backed by @generalcatalyst WIRED has the first external account of the company and the work:

items.title: @lanyon_ai：Formally verified magnetohydrodynamics, with provably hyperbolicity-preserving magnetic divergence error correction. Sim
items.abstract_or_text: Formally verified magnetohydrodynamics, with provably hyperbolicity-preserving magnetic divergence error correction. Simulating plasma vortices and supersonic plasma flows in arbitrary geometries using shock-capturing schemes for the equations of ideal MHD, all implemented and verified autonomously with Lanyon. ~32,000 lines of C, ~50,000 lines of Lean proof, ~150 correctness theorems, all generated in ~7 minutes. The ideal MHD equations couple the equations of hydrodynamics with Maxwell’s equations for electromagnetism to describe the interactions of perfectly conducting fluids with magnetic fields. As an elegant reduced-order description, the ideal MHD equations occur ubiquitously throughout heliophysics, geophysics, and astrophysical plasma physics, as well as in modeling the equilibrium and stability of nuclear fusion reactors. Solving these equations involves unique numerical and algorithmic challenges, including issues surrounding the preservation of divergence constraints for the magnetic field, as well as complex thermodynamic stability and wave-speed restrictions. Lanyon one-shotted an end-to-end formally verified solver for the ideal MHD equations, including a provably hyperbolicity-preserving divergence correction scheme based on the Dedner et al. approach, with fully executable mathematical, physical, and numerical correctness proofs. Then it ran a variety of complex numerical and physical validation simulations, and autonomously analyzed the results. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first ever fully formally verified divergence correction scheme for the MHD equations. GitHub link and technical deep dive below.👇

items.title: @Junioryu136689：Nature Biotechnology: drug discovery is moving from brute-force screening to intelligent search across chemical space. A
items.abstract_or_text: Nature Biotechnology: drug discovery is moving from brute-force screening to intelligent search across chemical space. A new open-source platform, AdaptiveFlow, makes ultralarge virtual screening dramatically more scalable. The numbers are wild: • 69 BILLION ready-to-dock molecules from Enamine REAL Space • Chemical space organized into an 18-dimensional property grid • Target-guided screening + optional active learning to focus compute on promising regions • >1,500 docking protocols supported • Near-linear scaling to 5.6 million vCPUs on AWS • Experimentally validated nanomolar inhibitors against FSP1 and PARP1 The key idea isn’t to dock every molecule. AdaptiveFlow learns where in a 69-billion-molecule chemical universe it is worth looking — turning ultralarge virtual screening from brute-force computation into an adaptive search problem. A pretty striking example of AI changing not just how molecules are generated, but how chemical space itself is explored. Nature Biotechnology, published Sept. 1, 2026.

items.title: @Aliaian：Autonomous agent trading will be one of the next major narratives, especially on Robinhood Chain. Logos is building the
items.abstract_or_text: Autonomous agent trading will be one of the next major narratives, especially on Robinhood Chain. Logos is building the thing that stops the agent from going completely off the rails once it has access to real money The problem with autonomous trading is that prompts aren’t real risk management. You can tell an agent "never use leverage" or "never put more than 10% into one stock," but frontier models hallucinate, misunderstand instructions and behave unpredictably That obviously doesn’t work when an agent controls a serious portfolio. Logos turns those instructions into hard, machine enforced portfolio mandates: > Maximum position sizes > Minimum cash balances > Approved assets > No leverage > Maximum order sizes > Exposure and concentration limits The agent can propose whatever trade it wants, but before execution Logos checks what the portfolio would look like after the trade. If one of the rules is broken, the trade is refused. The interesting part is how they prove the checker is actually enforcing the mandate correctly. Logos uses Aristotle, the automated theorem prover developed by @HarmonicMath, the AI math company co founded by @vladtenev, to help generate formal proofs around the trading rules. Those proofs are then independently checked by Lean
